q-15370.prompt:
A University Campus has a total of $@@g:a@@$ students.
At the beginning of the new semester at the University, flu affected $@@n:n0@@$ students. After $@@n:tau@@$ days, the number of students affected by the flu increases to $@@n:n1@@.$ To the nearest day, how long does it take for the flu-stricken campus population to reach $@@n:target@@$ students?

*Hint: You may assume that the number of students affected by the flu, $P(t),$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t\ge 0$ is the time, in days.*
q-15370.solution:
The rate at which the campus population affected by the flu, $P(t),$ changes is proportional to the difference between the total campus population and its current population affected. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the total population of the campus, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=@@g:a@@$ students, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(@@g:a@@-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{@@g:a@@-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{@@g:a@@-P} & =\int k\,dt \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@g:a@@-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $@@g:a@@-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$
Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}@@g:a@@-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ @@g:a@@-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ @@g:a@@-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =@@g:a@@-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial campus population affected by the flu was $@@n:n0@@$ students. So, we apply the initial condition $P(0)=@@n:n0@@,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0) & =@@n:n0@@ \\ @@g:a@@-K{e}^{0} & =@@n:n0@@ \\ @@g:a@@-K & =@@n:n0@@ \\ K & =@@g:K@@\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=@@g:a@@-@@g:K@@{e}^{-kt}
$$

We're also told that, after $@@n:tau@@$ days, the campus population affected by flu was $@@n:n1@@$ students. So, applying the condition $P(@@n:tau@@)=@@n:n1@@,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(@@n:tau@@) & =@@n:n1@@ \\ @@g:a@@-@@g:K@@{e}^{-@@n:tau@@k} & =@@n:n1@@ \\ @@g:a-n1@@ & =@@g:K@@{e}^{-@@n:tau@@k} \\ {e}^{-@@n:tau@@k} & =@@f:(a-n1)/K@@ \\ -@@n:tau@@k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-n1)/K@@) \\ k & =-\frac{1}{@@n:tau@@}\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-n1)/K@@)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let ${t}_{1}$ be the time when $@@n:target@@$ students are affected by the flu. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P({t}_{1}) & =@@n:target@@ \\ @@g:a@@-@@g:K@@{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =@@n:target@@ \\ @@n:a-target@@ & =@@g:K@@{e}^{-k{t}_{1}} \\ {e}^{-k{t}_{1}} & =@@f:(a-target)/K@@ \\ -k{t}_{1} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-target)/K@@) \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-target)/K@@).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that $@@n:target@@$ students will be affected by the flu after

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-target)/K@@)}{-\frac{1}{@@n:tau@@}\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-n1)/K@@)}=@@d3:result@@…≈@@i:result@@\,\text{days},
$$

rounded to the nearest day.

q-37389.prompt:
A poultry farmer has egg-laying chickens. She knows that her farm can produce a maximum of $@@n:a@@$ eggs a day; however, it is far behind it.
Since she started monitoring, the chickens laid $@@n:n1@@$ eggs and $@@n:n2@@$ eggs on days $@@n:t1@@$ and $@@n:t2@@$, respectively. How many eggs do the chickens lay on day $@@n:time@@$?
Round your answer to the nearest integer.

*Hint: You may assume that the egg production $E(t)$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t$ is the time, in days.*
q-37389.solution:
The rate at which the egg production $E(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum possible egg production and its current egg production. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dE}{dt}=k(a-E),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum production of the farm, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=@@n:a@@$ eggs, and we have

$$
\frac{dE}{dt}=k(@@n:a@@-E).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dE}{@@n:a@@-E} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dE}{@@n:a@@-E} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@n:a@@-E| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $@@n:a@@-E>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $E(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}@@n:a@@-E & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ @@n:a@@-E & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ @@n:a@@-E & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ E & =@@n:a@@-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on day $@@n:t1@@,$ the egg production was $@@n:n1@@$ eggs. So, applying the condition $E(@@n:t1@@)=@@n:n1@@,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E(@@n:t1@@) & =@@n:n1@@ \\ @@n:a@@-K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@k} & =@@n:n1@@ \\ K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@k} & =@@n:D0@@.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on day $@@n:t2@@,$ the egg production was $@@n:n2@@$ eggs. So, applying the condition $E(@@n:t2@@)=@@n:n2@@,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}E(@@n:t2@@) & =@@n:n2@@ \\ @@n:a@@-K{e}^{-@@n:t2@@k} & =@@n:n2@@ \\ K{e}^{-@@n:t2@@k} & =@@n:D2@@.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@k}}{K{e}^{-@@n:t2@@k}} & =\frac{@@n:D0@@}{@@n:D2@@} \\ {e}^{@@n:t1@@k} & =@@f:D0/D2@@ \\ @@n:t1@@k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:D0/D2@@) \\ k & =\frac{1}{@@n:t1@@}\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:D0/D2@@)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@\cdot (1/@@n:t1@@)\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)} & =@@n:D0@@ \\ K & =@@n:D0@@{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)} \\ K & =@@n:K@@\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $E(t):$

$$
E(t)=@@n:a@@-@@n:K@@{e}^{-(t/@@n:t1@@)\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)}
$$

Finally, the number of eggs laid on day $t=@@n:time@@$ is

$$
E(@@n:time@@)=@@n:a@@-@@n:K@@{e}^{-(@@n:time@@/@@n:t1@@)\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)}≈@@d3:result@@…≈@@i:result@@\,\text{eggs},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

q-37400.prompt:

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=@@n:k@@(@@g:a@@-P).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{@@g:a@@-P} & =@@n:k@@\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{@@g:a@@-P} & =\int @@n:k@@\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@g:a@@-P| & =@@n:k@@t+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $@@g:a@@-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$
Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}@@n:a@@-P & ={e}^{-@@n:k@@t-C} \\ @@n:a@@-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-@@n:k@@t} \\ @@c:a@@-P & =K{e}^{-@@n:k@@t} \\ P & =@@g:a@@-K{e}^{-@@n:k@@t}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the initial population of the school was $@@n:n0@@$ students. So, we apply the initial condition $P(0)=@@n:n0@@,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}@@n:n0@@ & =@@g:a@@-K{e}^{0} \\ @@n:n0@@ & =@@g:a@@-K \\ K & =@@g:K@@\end{aligned}

Therefore, the solution to our initial value problem is

$$
P(t)=@@g:a@@-@@g:K@@{e}^{-@@n:k@@t}.
$$

Finally, the population in the school after $t=@@n:time@@$ years is

$$
P(@@n:time@@)=@@g:a@@-@@g:K@@{e}^{-@@n:k@@\cdot @@n:time@@}≈@@i:result@@\,\text{students},

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{@@n:a@@-T} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{@@n:a@@-T} & =\int k\,dt \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@n:a@@-T| & =kt+C\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}@@n:a@@-T & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ @@n:a@@-T & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ @@n:a@@-T & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =@@n:a@@-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}

$$

$$
T(t)=@@n:a@@-@@n:K@@{e}^{-kt}.

Substituting the value of $k,$ we get:

$$
{t}_{1}=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-target)/K@@)}{-\frac{1}{@@n:tau@@}\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-n1)/K@@)}=@@d3:result@@…≈@@i:result@@\text{ }\text{minutes},

q-335590.solution:
The rate at which the bread production $E(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum possible bread production and its current bread production. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dE}{dt}=k(a-E),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum production of the bakery, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=@@n:a@@$ loaves, and we have

$$
\frac{dE}{dt}=k(@@n:a@@-E).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dE}{@@n:a@@-E} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dE}{@@n:a@@-E} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@n:a@@-E| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $@@n:a@@-E>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $E(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}@@n:a@@-E & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ @@n:a@@-E & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ @@n:a@@-E & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ E & =@@n:a@@-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on day $@@n:t1@@,$ the bread production was $@@n:n1@@$ loaves. So, applying the condition $E(@@n:t1@@)=@@n:n1@@,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E(@@n:t1@@) & =@@n:n1@@ \\ @@n:a@@-K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@k} & =@@n:n1@@ \\ K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@k} & =@@n:D0@@.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on day $@@n:t2@@,$ the bread production was $@@n:n2@@$ loaves. So, applying the condition $E(@@n:t2@@)=@@n:n2@@,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}E(@@n:t2@@) & =@@n:n2@@ \\ @@n:a@@-K{e}^{-@@n:t2@@k} & =@@n:n2@@ \\ K{e}^{-@@n:t2@@k} & =@@n:D2@@.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@k}}{K{e}^{-@@n:t2@@k}} & =\frac{@@n:D0@@}{@@n:D2@@} \\ {e}^{@@n:t1@@k} & =@@f:D0/D2@@ \\ @@n:t1@@k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:D0/D2@@) \\ k & =\frac{1}{@@n:t1@@}\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:D0/D2@@)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@\cdot (1/@@n:t1@@)\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)} & =@@n:D0@@ \\ K & =@@n:D0@@{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)} \\ K & =@@n:K@@\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $E(t):$

$$
E(t)=@@n:a@@-@@n:K@@{e}^{-(t/@@n:t1@@)\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)}
$$

Finally, the number of loaves baked on day $t=@@n:time@@$ is

$$
E(@@n:time@@)=@@n:a@@-@@n:K@@{e}^{-(@@n:time@@/@@n:t1@@)\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)}≈@@d3:result@@…≈@@i:result@@\,\text{loaves},
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

q-335619.prompt:
A national park is monitoring the number of people who have downloaded a new park app. The system can support a maximum of $@@n:a@@$ users, but the total is still below this limit. Since the park began tracking downloads, the number of users reached $@@n:n1@@$ on day $@@n:t1@@$ and $@@n:n2@@$ on day $@@n:t2@@.$ On what day will the number of users reach $@@n:target@@?$ Round your answer to the nearest integer.

*Hint: You may assume that the number of users, $P(t),$ increases at a rate that obeys an inhibited growth model, where $t$ is the time, in days.*
q-335619.solution:
The rate at which the number of app users $P(t)$ changes is proportional to the difference between the maximum population and its current population. Therefore, we have the inhibited growth equation

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(a-P),
$$

where $a$ is the maximum number of users the system can support, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $a=@@n:a@@$ users, and we have

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=k(@@n:a@@-P).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{@@n:a@@-P} & =k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dP}{@@n:a@@-P} & =\int k\,\text{d}t \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡|@@n:a@@-P| & =kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited growth equation, we have $@@n:a@@-P>0$ for all $t\ge 0.$ Next, we solve for $P(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}@@n:a@@-P & ={e}^{-kt-C} \\ @@n:a@@-P & ={e}^{-C}{e}^{-kt} \\ @@n:a@@-P & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ P & =@@n:a@@-K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{-C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that, on day $@@n:t1@@,$ the number of users was $@@n:n1@@.$ So, applying the condition $P(@@n:t1@@)=@@n:n1@@,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(@@n:t1@@) & =@@n:n1@@ \\ @@n:a@@-K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@k} & =@@n:n1@@ \\ K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@k} & =@@n:D0@@.\end{aligned}
$$

We're also told that, on day $@@n:t2@@,$ the number of users was $@@n:n2@@.$ So, applying the condition $P(@@n:t2@@)=@@n:n2@@,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(@@n:t2@@) & =@@n:n2@@ \\ @@n:a@@-K{e}^{-@@n:t2@@k} & =@@n:n2@@ \\ K{e}^{-@@n:t2@@k} & =@@n:D2@@.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, by dividing the result of the first condition by the result of the second, we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@k}}{K{e}^{-@@n:t2@@k}} & =\frac{@@n:D0@@}{@@n:D2@@} \\ {e}^{@@n:delta@@k} & =@@f:D0/D2@@ \\ @@n:delta@@k & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:D0/D2@@) \\ k & =\frac{1}{@@n:delta@@}\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:D0/D2@@)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting back into the result of the first condition, we solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}K{e}^{-@@n:t1@@\cdot (1/@@n:delta@@)\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)} & =@@n:D0@@ \\ K & =@@n:D0@@{e}^{(1/2)\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)} \\ K & =@@n:D0@@\sqrt{@@f:D0/D2@@} \\ K & =@@n:D0@@\cdot @@f:sqrt(D0/D2)@@ \\ K & =@@n:K@@\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $P(t):$

$$
P(t)=@@n:a@@-@@n:K@@{e}^{-(t/@@n:delta@@)\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@r:D0/D2@@)}.
$$

Finally, let $d$  be the day when the app reaches $@@n:target@@$ users. Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(d) & =@@n:target@@ \\ @@n:a@@-@@n:K@@{e}^{-kd} & =@@n:target@@ \\ @@n:a-target@@ & =@@n:K@@{e}^{-kd} \\ {e}^{-kd} & =\frac{@@n:a-target@@}{@@n:K@@} \\ {e}^{-kd} & =@@f:(a-target)/K@@ \\ -kd & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-target)/K@@) \\ d & =-\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-target)/K@@).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting in our value for $k,$ we conclude that the number of users will be $@@n:target@@$ on day

$$
d=\frac{-\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:(a-target)/K@@)}{\frac{1}{@@n:delta@@}\operatorname{ln}⁡(@@f:D0/D2@@)}=@@d4:result@@…≈@@i:result@@,
$$

rounded to the nearest day.
